Content: Right triangle trigonometry expands our mathematical study of triangles beyond Pythagorean theorem and special right triangles. Trigonometry bridges the gap between angles and sides, allowing us to calculate every single side length and angle measurement of a right triangle using just one side and one acute angle. In the real world, civil engineers use trigonometry to calculate the precise incline of a wheelchair ramp and astronomers use it to measure the immense distances to nearby stars.

On the SAT exam, right triangle trigonometry is an important component across the Geometry and Trigonometry section. These concepts evaluate our spatial reasoning and algebraic agility within the practical context of real-world problems. For example, certain SAT problems might give us the task of calculating the height of a flagpole based on the length of its shadow or ask for missing angles within figures on the coordinate plane. Mastering trigonometric relationships provides us with a precise toolkit to find direct algebraic solutions in situations where minimal information is given about a right Triangle.

Unlock right triangle trigonometry requires mastery of the vocabulary used to label the sides of a right triangle relative to a specific non-right angle, often denoted by the Greek letter `theta` (theta). No matter which angle we look at, the `ultext(Hypotenuse)` is always the same — it is the absolute longest side of the triangle and sits directly opposite the `90°` right angle. The identity of the remaining two sides, however, depends entirely on which acute angle we are working with. `ultext(Opposite Side)` describes the side that is directly across from the target angle `theta` and shares no common vertices with it. `ultext(Adjacent Side)` describe the side that runs right next to the target angle `theta` and connects with the hypotenuse to form the target angle.

Once these sides are properly identified, we can form a few different `ultext(Trigonometric Ratios)` — fundamental fractions comparing the lengths of two side of a right triangle. Because all triangles with the same angles angle are mathematically similar, these side ratios remain constant regardless of how big or small the side lengths actually are. The SAT exam covers the three primary trigonometric functions, which can be easily memorized using the acronym `ultext(SOH-CAH-TOA)`.

:ibox:• `ultext(Sine)` (`sintheta`) is the ratio of the length of the opposite side to the length of the hypotenuse.
• `ultext(Cosine)` (`costheta`) is the ratio of the length of the adjacent side to the length of the hypotenuse.
• `ultext(Tangent)` (`tantheta`) is the ratio of the length of the opposite side to the length of the adjacent side,.

In addition to these trigonometric ratios, some SAT problems also rely on the `ultext(Complementary Angle Theorem)` for sine and cosine equalities. Because the angles of a triangle sum to `180°` and the right angle is `90°`, the two remaining angles in a right triangle add up to `90°` (making them complementary). When switching between the two acute angles of a right triangle, the opposite side from one acute angle becomes the adjacent side to the other angle. This symmetry results in the sine of an acute angle always being perfectly equal to the cosine of its complementary angle. This identity can be expressed as `sin(x°)=cos(90°-x°)`.
